items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: mainly during my period with the Dizzy Gillespie quartet, quintet, big band, etcetera, my ten year association with Dizzy Gillespie

ctx.x: Can you remember specifically what it was about the Nat King Cole LP that grabbed your attention?

Monk, I don’t know — his voice, the music. What I can tell you is it was a trio: piano, bass and guitar. And I remember there was an album where he sang “When I Fall in Love,” “Mona Lisa,” “Our Love is Here to Stay.” I realized after I moved to the United States because before 1980 my English was zero. I didn’t know the meaning of “yes” so I learned to speak English here in the United States mainly during my period with the Dizzy Gillespie quartet, quintet, big band, etcetera, my ten year association with Dizzy…
So did you start paying more attention to the percussion end of things with Cuban music?

items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: he did just not talk to me about what he wanted me to play in his band, he taught me, it was a daily lesson about bebop vocabulary, about jazz, about life.

ctx.x: Well yes he did. Dizzy was the type, Dizzy, my dear friend, my father, my brother, Dizzy Gillespie was famous in the business for being a pain in the neck for drummers. He was

hard on drummers. So but Dizzy, aside from teaching me a lot about the bebop vocabulary, which I really appreciate because he did just not talk to me about what he wanted me to play in his band, he taught me, it was a daily lesson about bebop vocabulary, about jazz, about life. Yeah. He told me, “Ignacio,” for example when you arrive to Dizzy’s band he will handle you a huge 22 inch China cymbal that you have to play behind him because that was the sound he wanted to hear because the explanation was that the…
Yeah, you don’t know like what did I do?
